title: Cambridge academics reject university’s attempt to end row over Jason Arday
summary:
Group calls for ‘thorough and transparent investigation’ of hiring of professor who resigned after his claims came under scrutiny

The University of Cambridge has announced a review into the way it vets and hires senior academic staff in an effort to fend off external and internal criticism of its appointment of Jason Arday as a professor.

But a group of Cambridge academics quickly rejected the university’s response, saying: “We strongly believe that a thorough and transparent investigation into the wider circumstances of this damaging episode is essential.”

Continue reading...
full_text:
The University of Cambridge has announced a review into the way it vets and hires senior academic staff in an effort to fend off external and internal criticism of its appointment of Jason Arday as a professor.

But a group of Cambridge academics quickly rejected the university’s response, saying: “We strongly believe that a thorough and transparent investigation into the wider circumstances of this damaging episode is essential.”

Arday resigned earlier this week after mounting scepticism over his personal and professional claims, three-and-a-half years after he was acclaimed as Cambridge’s youngest black professor with a life story of educational disadvantage, including being unable to speak until the age of 11.

Cambridge sources said that university and college leaders had hoped Arday’s resignation would end the controversy. But internal anger has continued to grow over his appointment process and the threats to the university’s black staff from toxic media commentary.

In a statement issued on Friday, Cambridge said: “Jason Arday has resigned from his post at the university with immediate effect. Regardless of this, and for clarification, the university will continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday’s appointment and tenure.

“The findings will feed into a review of the process for the appointment of senior academic roles. In addition, and as previously stated, the university’s research policy committee will review the misconduct in research policy.”

The Guardian revealed on Thursday that Cambridge academics were demanding the university carry out a thorough investigation.

The letter sent on Friday to Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, highlights the “toxic and frequently racist commentary” that has accompanied much of the online and media coverage, adding: “These manifestly false claims have the potential to set back the modest progress Cambridge has made in addressing historical underrepresentation, and to deter any Black academic from applying for or accepting a position at the university in the future.”

Prentice became vice-chancellor of Cambridge in July 2023, after Arday’s appointment earlier that year.

The letter states: “We therefore ask that you appoint an independent body comprising senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge to address these issues, with a clear timeline for completing its work and a commitment to share its findings with the university and the public.”

The nearly 100 signatories are senior professors and Cambridge academics, including Suchitra Sebastian, a professor of physics, and Mónica Figueroa, a professor of sociology, as well as Timothy Gowers, a past winner of the Field medal for mathematics. Other prominent names include Nicholas Guyatt, a professor of North American history, Mary Laven, a professor of early modern history, Anuj Dawar, a professor of logic, and Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature.

The signatories want an independent investigation into the circumstances of Arday’s appointment, and any risk assessment made by the university’s management “when crafting a media narrative focusing on his youth, his race, and his transformative potential”.

It also wants details of the university’s handling of allegations of academic misconduct against Arday, including whether the university was involved in efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations.

The university has denied supporting Arday’s efforts to stop publication of critical coverage in the Times Higher magazine last year, or funding his use of lawyers.

The signatories also call for an evaluation of the “enormous damage this episode has done to people of colour within and beyond the Cambridge academic community, and what can be done immediately to reassure them – and the wider public – that anti-racism and academic integrity at Cambridge are both essential and mutually reinforcing.”

However, Cambridge’s Jesus College – where Arday was a fellow – has said it will drop its previously announced plans to carry out a parallel “process” to the university’s investigation first revealed on Wednesday evening.

A message to staff from Sonita Alleyne, the college’s master, said: “Because Professor Arday’s college fellowship was contingent on his university appointment, his resignation brought his fellowship to an end. The college’s acceptance of his resignation concludes the process announced in last night’s statement.

“This is a very difficult time for Professor Arday and his family. As he requested in his resignation letter, we hope that they are now afforded peace and privacy.”

One Cambridge academic said the message showed that the university wanted to “draw a line” under the affair in the hope that it would subside.

Arday’s resignation on Wednesday followed intense media scrutiny, beginning with accusations of plagiarism and followed by questions over a string of his claims ranging from endurance running and charity fundraising to confrontations with masked assailants.

Cambridge initially defended Arday as “the victim of a vile campaign” before announcing that it would conduct an internal investigation of “new information” regarding Arday, who then resigned shortly after.

On Friday night, the University of Glasgow said it would review its past appointment of Arday as a professor.

A university spokesperson said: “Jason Arday was employed as professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023.

“He left the university to take up his role as professorial chair at the University of Cambridge.

“The principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future.”

title: Primary schools to be told to identify children at risk of future unemployment
summary:
Exclusive: Neet crisis review to call for teachers to be asked to spot those at risk of leaving education jobless at 16

  • What can Dublin teach us? Milburn goes on quest to learn

Primary schools in England should be required to identify children at risk of leaving education at 16 without finding a job, a government review is to recommend.

Alan Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness, said he would call for sweeping changes in education policy alongside a shake-up of the benefits system to address the problem.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Primary schools in England should be required to identify children at risk of leaving education at 16 without finding a job, a government review is to recommend.

Alan Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness, said he would call for sweeping changes in education policy alongside a shake-up of the benefits system to address the problem.

Speaking to the Guardian, he said ministers needed to “make somebody responsible” for identifying and supporting the children who risked becoming Neet (not in employment, education or training) after their GCSE year up to the age of 24.

“The warning signs are there from a very early, early age. You know, frankly from preschool,” he said.

“So, definitely primary schools should be identifying children who are at risk of being Neet. And secondary schools and other services should be intercepting, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path.”

In an interview during a visit to Dublin this week, the former Labour health secretary said the recommendation would form part of his final report into Britain’s youth worklessness crisis, which is expected this autumn.

Britain’s young adults are bearing the brunt of a rise in unemployment, with the number of 16 to 24-year-olds who are Neet surpassing a million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade.

Representing as many as one in eight young people, the rate has swelled at a significantly faster rate than in other countries amid a sharp rise in mental ill-health and a tough jobs market.

Milburn’s review comes as Andy Burnham puts tackling the crisis in youth employment at the top of his agenda for government, including changes in his first weeks as prime minister to retool technical education and apprenticeships.

Labour is also gearing up for a fresh tilt at welfare reform amid concerns over a spiralling benefits bill and the hit to the economy and people’s lives from a prolonged period out of work.

Milburn said welfare reform would form a critical plank of his final report, but cautioned that any steps to restrict benefit payments for young people would need to be accompanied by higher levels of education, health and job support.

He said that by the time a young person reached the benefit system it represented an “upstream failure” in education, skills and health policy because a functioning system could have helped them to find a job.

“I think we’ve got to turbocharge that education; that support. We’ve got to turbocharge opportunities for young people; we’ve got to make it easier for young people to get a job,” he said.

“And alongside opportunities, of course, there has got to be some obligations. Of course.”

Burnham has said he is determined to reform the welfare system as part of his efforts to fix Britain’s dismal track record on youth employment, but would also provide more support for young people.

Speaking on a fact-finding mission to the Republic of Ireland, which has recorded the fastest fall in Neet rates in the EU over the past decade, Milburn said that far too often youth disengagement began long before the age of 16.

Suggesting that it can start before a child even reaches the school gates, he highlighted a study in Bradford that found children who were not school-ready at the age of 4 to 5 were almost three times as likely to become Neet by the time they reached the age of 16 to 17.

“We know what the correlated factors are [for a child at risk of becoming Neet] – whether that is poverty; mental health, or being in care. What we don’t do is take that knowledge and turn it into action.”

Under the proposal to be outlined in his final report, schools in England would be expected to flag a child’s risk of becoming Neet from the end of primary school, including by drawing on attendance records.

The Department for Education would also be asked to refresh its pupil premium guidance to emphasise that the extra money schools in England receive for supporting the most disadvantaged children could be used for tutoring and mentoring schemes for those at risk of becoming Neet.

Official figures show rates of school absence have ballooned since the Covid pandemic, with the number of pupils persistently absent – missing at least a 10th of school time – almost doubling to 1.3 million pupils in 2024 and 2025. Rates of severe absence – missing half of class time – and persistent absenteeism have also dramatically increased.

Milburn’s interim report in May warned that persistent absenteeism was associated with a 3.9 times greater risk of a young person being Neet by the time they reached the age of 16 to 18, and a 6.3 times greater risk of a young person being locked out of earning or learning for a sustained period.

While some schools have strategies using so-called “Roni” (risk of Neet indicator) tools, the practice is not widespread or mandated.

“We’ve got to get upstream because what we’re doing is we’re paying – this country, and young people – are paying the price of failure,” said Milburn.

title: With their assault on science, Trumpists aren’t just harming America – they’re harming themselves | Jan-Werner Müller
summary:
The administration is subjugating science to political imperatives, a major blow to US soft power and technological progress

The Trump administration is waging an unprecedented war on institutions devoted to research and higher learning. While plenty of countries have harmed universities by imposing neoliberal logics on academia – creating artificial markets in the name of spurring professors to be more productive – the Trumpist subjugation of all science to political imperatives has no equivalent in a democracy; if anything, it is reminiscent of Stalin’s Soviet Union. The assault now also targets foreign students and any kind of international collaboration – a major blow to US soft power. Why are Trumpists engaging in what can only be described as an act of wanton self-injury?

Project 2025’s Russell Vought, the director of the office of management and budget, initiated the rule change that would make any federal grant subject to review by political appointees – including funds for science that so far have been allocated through judgment by first-rate fellow scientists. This measure would furnish Trumpists with a new weapon to threaten universities along the lines of: “Nice medical school you have there – pity if something were to happen to it because your administration had failed to come into alignment with the president’s priorities.”

Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University

Continue reading...
full_text:
The Trump administration is waging an unprecedented war on institutions devoted to research and higher learning. While plenty of countries have harmed universities by imposing neoliberal logics on academia – creating artificial markets in the name of spurring professors to be more productive – the Trumpist subjugation of all science to political imperatives has no equivalent in a democracy; if anything, it is reminiscent of Stalin’s Soviet Union. The assault now also targets foreign students and any kind of international collaboration – a major blow to US soft power. Why are Trumpists engaging in what can only be described as an act of wanton self-injury?

Project 2025’s Russell Vought, the director of the office of management and budget, initiated the rule change that would make any federal grant subject to review by political appointees – including funds for science that so far have been allocated through judgment by first-rate fellow scientists. This measure would furnish Trumpists with a new weapon to threaten universities along the lines of: “Nice medical school you have there – pity if something were to happen to it because your administration had failed to come into alignment with the president’s priorities.”

Then there is the strategy recently presented by Trump’s science adviser, a former employee of Peter Thiel, with the unique distinction of having no relevant experience in research whatsoever. Michael Kratsios wants to shift decision-making from experts in universities to private corporations, which, helped by AI, are supposedly better positioned to spot potential breakthroughs. This constitutes a major break with the enormously successful approach the US took after the second world war: pour taxpayer money into basic, open-ended science which no private company would risk sponsoring – but with both citizens and American capital eventually benefiting from the inventions that came out of fundamental research. Kratsios wishes the government to adopt “the intentionality of a serious investor” in order to usher in a new “golden age of science” (declaring something “golden” seems enough to succeed in Trump-world). De facto, as critics have rightly pointed out, this seems a strategy to take money from what Trumpists perceive as their political enemies – universities – and shovel it to their allies in tech.

Meanwhile, the more directly ideological assault on universities continues. Having failed to tempt select institutions of higher learning with a “compact” to receive preferential federal treatment last year, Linda McMahon, the fake-wrestling-executive-turned-anti-education secretary, is now asking university presidents to pledge allegiance to the administration through statements on their websites: among other things, they are supposed to explain how they will increase “intellectual pluralism” (read: affirmative action for conservatives); deal with campus protest (read: police student speech the Trump administration does not like); and make education more provincial (serving America first) and instrumental (only immediate employability and vocational credentialism count) – and less critical of “our civilizational inheritance”.

In the spirit of Stephen Miller-type nativism, international donors are targeted no less than international collaboration in general; visas for PhD students are now limited to four years (an unrealistic time frame for many academic subjects), with possible extensions if students spend time and money on appealing to the Department of Homeland security (instead of doing actual research). The fact that many researchers in the past have stayed in the US after obtaining their doctorates, contributing to national wealth (just like America Firsters would presumably want) or went back to their countries with good feelings to the US – all that counts for nothing.

What explains such self-harm? Rightwing hostility to higher education is nothing new: from intellectuals supposedly being communist eggheads in the 1950s, to moral panics about “political correctness” in the 1990s and “wokeness” in recent years, there is the basic stance made explicit by JD Vance in 2021: “Universities are the enemy.” But Trump’s rule has brought together a novel coalition, one divided by many issues but united in their desire to destroy universities as we know them. Among them: the Maga hardcore with its traditional anti-intellectualism and nativism; the Silicon Valley oligarchs who imagine their companies replacing (and monetizing) university functions; and conservatives in name, but radicals in practice who want to take over higher education, but, failing that, would like to burn the whole system down.

Also novel, in the wake of Covid, is the commitment of so many on the right to the idea that, somehow, science and freedom are opposites, that not having ever to listen to people who know something better than you do is the essence of personal liberation. If that emotional fuel for the new anti-intellectualism were not powerful enough, there is a highly flammable desire for revenge – amply on display in the endless attacks on Anthony Fauci.

To be sure, Congress has not gone along with some of the major funding cuts for science Trump keeps requesting; even Republican politicians quietly resist when monies would stop flowing to their districts. And the new OMB rule, it seems, is being blocked in a funding deal reached in the Senate this week. But one cannot rely on such occasional pushback by one Republican or another, because none of them has offered a principled defense of the postwar model (in fact, given the conduct of the likes of the senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn this week, it seems fair to say that “principled Republican” is fast becoming a contradiction in terms).

University leaders and prominent scientists have to hold the line in opposing possible “deals” with the Trump administration; everyone could have learned by now that Trumpists will not stick to their end of the bargain. More importantly, those seeing things wrong with peer review, for instance, or too much administrative busywork for researchers – and some of these problems are real – have to realize that Trumpists are the last who can be trusted to solve them.

title: How HBCUs Are Redefining Student Success
summary:
How HBCUs Are Redefining Student Success
Joshua.Bay Fri, 08/07/2026 - 03:00 AM

From helping stopped-out students return to creating faster routes to graduate school, HBCUs are removing barriers at every stage of college.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Historically Black colleges and universities have received growing national attention in recent years as applications and enrollment have climbed. But across many campuses, another shift is underway: HBCUs are redesigning the systems that help students persist and graduate.

Recent initiatives that HBCUs have made to remove barriers to student success range from helping stopped-out students return and expanding course access to reducing nontuition costs and creating faster routes into professional degrees.

Here are four ways HBCUs are supporting student success.

Reducing financial and basic needs barriers.

As college affordability continues to challenge students nationwide, rising costs for housing, food and other basic needs are increasingly influencing whether students enroll and ultimately complete their degrees. In response, Coppin State University is reducing nontuition expenses for students who live on campus.

Beginning this fall, the public, historically Black university in Baltimore will lower meal plan costs by 12 percent through a newly negotiated food service agreement. The university will also keep mandatory student fees flat, part of a broader effort to reduce financial barriers, limit student debt and support degree completion.

Following the new food service agreement, Coppin’s annual board cost will be roughly $4,875—less than that of every other four-year institution in Maryland. By comparison, annual board costs at other public universities are $6,290 at Towson University, $6,564 at Bowie State University and $6,820 at the University of Maryland, College Park.

Coppin President Anthony Jenkins said the cost reduction reflects the institution’s commitment to boosting affordability through strategic financial management and operational efficiencies. He added that rising food costs and growing concerns about basic needs insecurity among college students helped inform the university’s decision.

“What we’re trying to do is reduce the barriers that affect our students’ ability to focus on why they’re here,” Jenkins said. “That’s academics, building lifelong friendships and developing into the scholars we want them to become.”

Keeping students on track for graduation.

Course availability has long been a barrier to college completion, forcing some students to delay graduation when required classes aren’t offered—or even transfer elsewhere to stay on track.

In response, eHBCU, a group of six historically Black colleges and universities that joined forces last year, announced a new course-sharing partnership in June that allows students to remain enrolled at their home institution while accessing courses offered at other participating HBCUs.

The consortium, led by Delaware State University, partnered with the online course-sharing company Acadeum to support the initiative. Through the partnership, students can enroll in approved online courses offered by another eHBCU member without transferring institutions or losing progress toward their degree.

Participating institutions include Delaware State University, Southern University and A&M College, Southern University at Shreveport, Southern University at New Orleans, Alabama State University, and Pensole Lewis College of Business & Design.

Terry Jeffries, executive director of eHBCU, said the initiative was designed to address how lack of course availability can affect graduation timelines and student retention, particularly for adult and nontraditional learners balancing work, family or geographic constraints.

“That was one of the reasons we partnered with [Acadeum],” Jeffries said. “To support students wherever they are in their journey, while still ensuring they can remain connected to an HBCU experience.”

Re-engaging students who stop out.

Historically Black colleges and universities have seen growing interest from students and increased investment in their missions in recent years. But for many HBCUs, longstanding resource challenges and the barriers students face outside the classroom continue to create obstacles to college completion.

A new report from InsideTrack found that a five-year coaching initiative across 39 HBCUs boosted attainment among both current and stopped-out students. Stopped-out students who received coaching re-enrolled at a rate of 6.9 percent—2.5 times the national average—with more than 1,300 returning to their institutions during the five-year period.

Among actively enrolled students, those who met with a coach retained at a rate of 90.4 percent from fall to spring, compared with 82.4 percent for students who did not complete a coaching meeting.

Coaches used personalized outreach and one-on-one sessions to help students clarify their goals, identify barriers, and navigate financial, academic and administrative challenges that could interrupt their paths to completion.

Henri LaSane, associate vice president of HBCU programs at InsideTrack, said the initiative was built around the understanding that students’ paths to completion are rarely linear and that institutions must provide support when challenges arise.

“When we look at the journey and the life cycle of a student, it’s not a straight line,” LaSane said. “Unexpected curves happen, and those things can oftentimes derail and unintentionally impact our belief and ability to re-enroll and persist.”

Helping graduates move into professional education and careers.

As concerns about college affordability and student debt continue to rattle higher education, institutions are increasingly exploring accelerated degree pathways that allow students to reach their career goals more quickly and at a lower cost.

Grambling State University and Southern University Law Center announced in June a new 3+3 Accelerated Law Program that will allow eligible students to earn a bachelor’s degree and a law degree in six years, rather than the traditional seven. University leaders said the pathway is designed to reduce barriers to legal education by providing structured advising, early exposure to the legal profession and a guaranteed admissions pathway for students who meet program requirements.

Grambling State President Martin Lemelle said students can expect to save between $16,000 and $18,000 in tuition and fees by completing their undergraduate and law degrees in six years.

Connie Walton, provost and vice president for academic affairs, said university officials estimate total savings could reach roughly $100,000 when housing, meals and other educational expenses are included.

“That’s a huge savings,” Walton said. “Then, when you consider that students will likely apply to fewer law schools, there are additional savings associated with reduced application fees.”

title: Star Sociology Professor Resigns After Cambridge Opens Investigation
summary:
Star Sociology Professor Resigns After Cambridge Opens Investigation
Susan H. Greenberg Fri, 08/07/2026 - 03:00 AM

Jason Arday, the youngest Black professor ever appointed at Cambridge, has quit amid allegations of plagiarism and academic misconduct.

Byline(s)
Tom Williams for Times Higher Education
full_text:
Sociology professor Jason Arday has announced he is leaving his role at the University of Cambridge after facing questions over his academic work.

The scholar announced his resignation, effective immediately, in an open letter published by the Good Law Project hours after the institution announced it was going to investigate him owing to “new information” coming to light.

Arday, the youngest Black professor ever appointed by Cambridge, has faced a series of allegations in recent days, including claims he plagiarized part of his Ph.D. thesis and some material that appeared in journal papers.

Affiliations with universities including Glasgow and Ohio State have also been questioned after the institutions denied any ongoing links with the professor.

Arday said he had faced “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary” that “have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love.”

“I have tried to continue because I believe deeply in the values of higher education, in rigorous scholarship, and in the transformative power of universities,” he added.

“I have tried because of my students, my colleagues and the countless people who have written to tell me that my journey gave them hope. But there comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great.”

Arday said he wanted to “reclaim some peace, some privacy and some semblance of an ordinary life” and I “have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away.”

He said the decision “should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge” or “an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me.”

“It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.”

He promised that it was “not the end of my work” and “I will return stronger, wiser and with the same determination that has always defined my journey.”

Earlier, Cambridge said it had begun an investigation “following new information about Professor Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments.”

“In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded.”

Cambridge said “a number” of complaints had been made regarding academic misconduct and these were being handled “in line with our misconduct in research policy.”

The university had previously said concerns relating to Arday’s Ph.D. thesis were a matter for the awarding institution, Liverpool John Moores University, which has cleared Arday of plagiarism.

Arday has admitted making “mistakes” and told The Times he should be held “accountable” but has denied being a “liar and fantasist.”

Cambridge said it was “fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter,” adding that it “remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both university policies and employment law.”

“We also fully recognize that there is a person at the center of this situation, and we continue to provide support to him.”

Arday is also now the subject of a separate investigation at Jesus College, where he was a fellow.

Times Higher Education journalist Jack Grove was also looking into allegations that Arday had plagiarized parts of his Ph.D. thesis when he received a call from the Metropolitan Police, who said a complaint had been made against him. He was told the matter had been closed but warned not to try to contact Arday again, because it was affecting Arday’s mental health.

Writing for THE, Grove said that he was “shocked” to receive the call, noting that he had not contacted the professor for months.

title: Clemson, UF, UVU and other colleges get new leaders
summary: We’re rounding up July’s leadership transitions, including two public colleges that faced unexpected hurdles when installing new presidents.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Editor’s note: The Leadership Ledger is a monthly roundup of some of the most noteworthy college leadership changes nationwide.

For many colleges, July is when long-planned leadership transitions come to fruition. But a handful of institutions experienced a more disheveled start to the new academic year.

Clemson University had to quickly pivot after its already-announced incoming president reversed his decision to accept the role. The University of Florida finally installed its leadership pick after a skirmish with system officials. And the College of the Florida Keys abruptly fired its president and is now facing allegations that officials violated open meetings law over the speed and opacity of the decision.

Below, we’re rounding up some of last month’s biggest leadership changes.

President: Stuart Bell

Institution: University of Florida

Coming or going? Coming

Stuart Bell became president of UF on July 1,following a delayed and chaotic process that gave many déjà vu.

In May, UF's presidential search committee recommended Bell, the former president of the University of Alabama, as the sole finalist to lead the university. The governing board of the State University System of Florida originally planned to vote on his confirmation in June.

But board Chair Alan Levine delayed Bell’s confirmation at the last minute, citing concerns the UF board was out of compliance with the system’s governance regulations. The university board disputed those allegations and sought to work around the setback by naming Bell as interim leader on June 22.

Throughout the process, Bell also faced a conservative campaign against his selection over his previous diversity, equity and inclusion work at UA. Last year, the Florida system’s governing board voted againstconfirmingSanta Ono, former president of the University of Michigan, as UF’s new leader amid a similar coordinated push.

The system’s governing board ultimately held Bell's confirmation vote a week after it was initially scheduled, and Bell took the helm of UF effective immediately.He is the university's first permanent president in almost two years.

President: Jeremiah Shinn

Institution: University of Montana

Coming or going? Coming

Jeremiah Shinn became the 20th president of the University of Montana on July 1. The public flagship's board of regents named Shinn, then the interim president at Boise State University, as its next leader in April following an “expedited and comprehensive” search process.

Shinn replaced Seth Bodnar, who abruptly stepped down as the university's president in January amid rumors he would run for U.S. Senate.Bodnar formally announced his candidacy two months later.

In the roughly five months between Bodnar's departure and Shinn's first day, the University of Montana did not have a formal leader.Montana Commissioner of Higher Education Clay Christiantold Montana Public Radio in January that an interim president would not be necessary and that he would help manage the campus in the meantime.

President: David Hahn

Institution: Boise State University

Coming or going? Coming

The Idaho State Board of Education on July 1 unanimouslyconfirmed David Hahn as the next president of Boise State University,following his selection as the sole finalist for the role the month prior.

Hahn, previously the dean of engineering at the University of Arizona,assumed the role immediately after the board's vote despite having not yet relocated to Idaho. Under his contract, he has until Aug. 10 to begin working on campus, the board said.

Boise State's last permanent leader, Marlene Tromp, departed in May 2025 to lead the University of Vermont.

President: Benjamin Ayers

Institution: Clemson University

Coming or going? Coming

Clemson's trustee board on July 9 named Benjamin Ayers as the public institution's next president. The news came just days after Kevin Guskiewicz shocked the sector by announcing he would keep his job as president of Michigan State University rather than lead Clemson as previously planned.

In May, Clemson had selected Guskiewicz as its next permanent leaderwith a yet-to-be-finalized start date.But on July 6, Guskiewicz recommitted to MSU and told the campus community he had "productive conversations" with leaders of the public university's board about concerns he had raised in his initial departure letter.

Ayers, previously the University of Georgia's provost, became Clemson's president on Aug. 1.

Kim Wilkerson, chair of Clemson's board, said Ayers had been a "distinguished" candidate for the role during the university's initial search. But he had "stepped back from consideration in order to remain fully committed to the University of Georgia" before the board's final decision, she said.

"When circumstances changed, conversations resumed and the Board quickly affirmed what had become clear throughout the search: Dr. Ayers’ experience and vision made him the unanimous choice to serve as Clemson’s next president," Wilkerson said in a July 9 letter to the South Carolina campus.

President: Jon Anderson

Institution: Utah Valley University

Coming or going? Coming

Jon Anderson will be Utah Valley University's next president, per a July 17 announcement. He joins the institution from Pennsylvania Western University,where he has served as president since 2024.

Anderson will assume his new role on Aug. 10.

Astrid Tuminez, the university's last permanent leader, retired in May. Her decision came after a violent and contentious year at UVU marked by the on-campus killing of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk in September. UVU Provost Wayne Vaught had served as its interim president since then.

President: The College of the Florida Keys

Institution: Jonathan Gueverra

Coming or going? Going

CFK’s governing board abruptly fired President Jonathan Gueverra during a special July 20 meeting. The agenda listed only two items, one of which was "Presidents' Contracts."It did not indicate the board's intention to vote on Gueverra's continued employmentat the public institution, and the minutes do not give a reason for Gueverra's termination.

The meeting was called with only 72 hours’ notice, according to Keys Weekly, and board documents indicate that Gueverra was not in attendance.

Wayne LaRue Smith, a lawyer representing Gueverra, raised objections at the meeting over how little notice and information the board gave the ousted president. Smith also alleged the board's actions violate Florida's open meetings law and said Gueverra intends to seek a formal hearing before the state's administrative agency to challenge his termination, according to meeting minutes.

The board named Brittany Snyder, the college's chief financial officer, as interim president.

title: Brooks and Capehart on what progressive primary wins mean for Democrats
summary: David Brooks of The Atlantic and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW join Amna Nawaz to discuss the week in politics, including how progressive wins in Michigan could signal a leftward turn in the Democratic Party's base, congressional Republicans facing allegations of misconduct and President Trump's latest moves against birthright citizenship.
full_text:
Amna Nawaz:

Progressive wins in Michigan could signal a leftward turn in the Democratic Party's base. And, in Washington, some congressional Republicans face allegations of misconduct.

On those topics and more, we turn now to the analysis of Brooks and Capehart. That's "The Atlantic"'s David Brooks and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW.

Great to see you both.

Jonathan Capehart:

Hey, Amna.

David Brooks:

Good to see you.

Amna Nawaz:

A few new anecdotes from this week that I'm going to try to put to you, and you can divine the party's direction for Democrats moving forward here.

Start with this. In Missouri this week, we saw the moderate candidate there, Wesley Bell, defeat the progressive Cori Bush in a congressional primary rematch. But there are signs, as we mentioned, of an ascendant progressive wing. In Wisconsin, the front-runner in next week's Democratic gubernatorial primary is a Democratic Socialist. That's Francesca Hong.

And of course, in Michigan, as we have been covering all this week, the progressive Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic Senate primary, beating the moderate Haley Stevens. You may have already seen just today the Republican candidate in that case -- in that race, rather, Mike Rogers, released this video, trying to appeal directly to those Stevens voters. Take a listen.

Mike Rogers (R), Michigan Senatorial Candidate: To the vast majority of people across Michigan who do not want to throw their support behind a campaign filled with anger, divisiveness, calls for violence, and the views that are out of touch with your values, well, you have a home with us.

The fight is far greater than just left versus right. The fight is for the very soul of our nation.

Amna Nawaz:

Jonathan, are Democrats worried that more centrist Democrats in Michigan could decide to turn towards the Republican in this case?

Jonathan Capehart:

Well, sure. And I would say even, without that terrible ad, that they should be, because Haley -- keep in mind, Dr. El-Sayed won the nomination, but barely. This was not a blowout. This was a squeaker. And so he needs those folks who voted for Haley Stevens to vote for him.

Now, I have said from the beginning, former Congressman Mike Rogers is going to be a tough candidate, no matter who -- an opponent, no matter who the nominee was, whether it's Haley Stevens or Dr. El-Sayed. But that ad shows just how ugly and nasty this fight is going to be.

Amna Nawaz:

In terms of that, David, what we have seen from Republicans on the messaging front so far is some anti-Muslim rhetoric already. Republicans are now using Dr. El-Sayed's full name in their ads, which they haven't used before, which is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, which I guess is supposed to scare people or something.

But the president is also talking about a rising communism threat. None of these candidates are communists. Are those the strongest messages the Republicans have right now?

David Brooks:

No, they should just say, these people are too left-wing for you.

The Democrats are doing the same thing they did in 2020. They're angry at Trump. I understand that. They're angry at their own leaders for not standing up to Trump in the way they think he should be stood up to. And so they're swinging left.

In 2020, it was moderately left. If you remember the Democratic primary debate, presidential debate, almost all the candidates said, I believe in open borders. That was political suicide. This is political suicide times 10, because if you look, for example, there are 16 Democrats who have won in Trump districts, where Trump also won.

What do those 16 Democrats have in common? They're all moderates. This is one of the firmest pieces of research across the board, massive amounts of evidence. Moderates do better than progressives. They do better in race after race and race by an average of maybe four points.

And so if you want to win and defeat Republicans, nominate a moderate. It's not that complicated. You take a look at what happened in Georgia a couple of years ago. You had Raphael Warnock, a moderate, and Stacey Abrams, a progressive. Warnock wins, Abrams loses. It's the case over and over and over and again.

But Democrats seem to have not learned this message, at least the kind of voters who voted for El-Sayed. He did very well in highly educated and more elite districts. He, like all socialists, did very poorly among workers. In the general election, there are going to be a lot more people without college degrees than with college degrees, or at least in this primary campaign.

So this is bad news for Democratic electability.

Jonathan Capehart:

I would just say Dr. El-Sayed is not a socialist. He's a progressive, just to be clear. He's not a member of the DSA.

Amna Nawaz:

He's backed by many Democratic Socialists.

Jonathan Capehart:

Well, sure, he's backed by, but he's not like Mayor Mamdani, who is a member of the DSA.

And I would push back on David. It's not just anger at Trump. It's anger at Trump policies. It's not just we don't like the president because he is who he is. We don't like the president, particularly in Michigan, because of the tariffs, because of the war. There are lots of tangible Trump policies that Dr. El-Sayed ran on to get people's votes.

And that message that he's -- he argued during the campaign is one he's going to take to the general election. And it's just a matter of whether it will penetrate. And that's the big test here.

David Brooks:

Voters in almost every presidential race, I think, in every one of my lifetime, have always said, who's closer to the center? And they vote for that person. Trump seemed closer to the center than Kamala Harris. Biden seemed closer to the center than Donald Trump.

Donald Trump over the last few years has run away from the center. He is handing this election to the Democrats. All they have to do is sit there and be couch potatoes. They do not have to support Medicare for all so that Republicans can go to them and say, you like your private health insurance? Mr. El-Sayed's going to take that away from you.

That is politically bad news, and that's only one of the issues on which the party is moving further and further away from the center, and therefore...

Jonathan Capehart:

I mean, I disagree that the Democratic Party writ large is moving far away from the center, and that a few races won by Democratic Socialists or people who identify as progressive, like Dr. El-Sayed, that -- to me, I just don't -- I do not see it that you can put this -- make this blanket argument that the Democratic Party is running far left.

Amna Nawaz:

We will see what happens when voters have a chance to speak on this.

Jonathan Capehart:

And that is the key thing. It's the voters who have made these decisions.

Amna Nawaz:

I know you both are following these other headlines as well, which is a new round of political misconduct stories that we are covering.

And let me just run through a few of these that I know folks have seen in our coverage. The Republican Congressman Chuck Edwards of North Carolina ended his reelection bid after an Ethics Committee found that he harassed two of his aides. In Ohio, of course, you have the Republican Congressman Max Miller there refusing to drop out, even as he faces abuse allegations from his ex-wife.

And his ex-father-in-law, former father-in-law, Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno, is telling him to step down. And, in Florida, there's Congressman Cory Mills, who's been accused of assault and is under investigation, is also staying in the race.

Jonathan, we should point out Democrats did force out Eric Swalwell after a slew of allegations. They took a few weeks to unite around pushing out Graham Platner, but how are you looking at these allegations now?

Jonathan Capehart:

Well, I mean, I'm looking at it like this. Miller's decided to stay, not to heed the president's advice to not run or whatever. The other -- the last member you mentioned is also sticking -- sticking with it. And I think...

Amna Nawaz:

Cory Mills, yes.

Jonathan Capehart:

Cory -- yes.

I think they have themselves to blame. They just look at what then-candidate Donald Trump did in 2016, when credible accusations of sexual misconduct that were leveled against him by multiple women, then the infamous grab them by the expletive recording that came out in October of 2016, and yet he still -- folks still stayed with him.

Like, he brazened it out. He withstood all the criticism, all the calls for him to get out, and he became president. So, if you're a Republican who's found himself in this situation, why wouldn't you think that I can -- if the president can do it, then why can't I? And that's exactly what they're doing.

And Republicans, again, I think have themselves to blame for this.

Amna Nawaz:

David, the House speaker, Mike Johnson, says he's not going to intervene, right? Do you think you should?

David Brooks:

Absolutely.

You know, he's running a body that should have some integrity. And some of these scandals are perennial scandals. There are always going to be financial scandals. They're going to -- men are going to be idiots and there are going to be sex abuse scandals, and they should all go for that.

But what worries me is the rise of bullyism, is the number of candidates who have either because of Trump or because they hate Trump, frankly, if you throw Graham Platner in there, they have decided that bullying is fine. And Max Miller seems to be the perfect example of this, rich kid who had a temper and still apparently has a temper, and who has half the U.S. Senate against him.

And that bullying, we know where that cultural vibe comes from. That does come from the White House. And it's become acceptable to be a bully in all sorts of noxious ways. And Mike Johnson should say, who's not a bully -- he seems to be a good guy, good Christian guy. He should say, no, we actually don't stand for this.

And, of course, then they'd say, well, what about Donald Trump? And he'd have to dance around that. But at least he can -- he can control the culture in his own organization.

Amna Nawaz:

Before I let you go, I want to get both of you quickly on the president's latest move, which are two new executive orders related to birthright citizenship.

This follows the Supreme Court striking down his previous effort to undermine this in -- from the 14th Amendment of the Constitution. He's got these two new orders more narrow in what they're targeting here. But I just want to ask each of you, why do you think the president is so singularly obsessed with this one issue?

Jonathan?

Jonathan Capehart:

Well, multiple times at this table during the campaign, I said the president was running an openly racist, xenophobic, white nationalist campaign for president.

And key in that campaign was doing something about immigration. It wasn't just about sealing the border. It was about stopping immigration from countries that messed with the demographic makeup of this country. There are a lot of people who fear the browning of America.

And by going after immigration so aggressively, he's trying to do something about that. So I am not surprised the president is looking at what the Supreme Court did and is trying to figure out ways to still try to accomplish his goal, whether it runs afoul of the Supreme Court decision or not. I don't think he really cares.

I think he's really just trying to do everything he can to stop immigration and in the process change the nature of who we are as a country.

David Brooks:

I have -- Trump supporters I spoke to say birthright citizenship was fine between 1925 and 1965, a low immigration era. Now we're in a high immigration era. They think the fundamental coherence of the culture is being weakened.

And that's their argument, and they're really upset about it. They think it's an existential threat, which I think Trump shares that, and that's why he's going back to this issue again and again and again. The only thing I'd point out, if you ask Americans by large majorities, they support immigration, right now, larger than majorities than any time in the last 10 years.

If you ask Americans, should America be a more diverse country or a less diverse country, you get like three-quarters of the people saying we want to be a more diverse country. So those people who think we should shut down birthright citizenship in order to create coherence instead of diversity, they're in a pretty small minority in this country.

Amna Nawaz:

America's figuring out who she is.

(Laughter)

Amna Nawaz:

Jonathan Capehart, David Brooks, thank you so much.

Jonathan Capehart:

Thanks, Amna.

David Brooks:

Thank you.

title: From playing games to building rockets: Portugal's Ubbu brings coding to primary school
summary: Just a day before the summer holidays, excitement fills the air at Lisbon's PaRK International School.
full_text:
Yet one last lesson has the pupil’s full attention in a primary school class . Tablets in hand, they navigate colourful games, solve puzzles or explore the International Space Station. They are learning coding through Ubbu, a Portuguese computer programming platform for children aged six to fourteen.

"It looks like they're playing games, but they're actually working on lots of different things," says teacher Teresa Cary. "They need to understand how to use a computer, how to make a robot do something. They need logic, it's actually maths."

Ubbu was developed by Code for All, a startup founded in 2015 by João Magalhães and a group of friends.

"We believed no one was prepared for the speed at which technology was entering our lives," he says. "We built a solution for any teacher, school or government that wanted to introduce digital literacy, computational thinking, creativity, and now AI and cybersecurity."

Available in four languages, ubbu now reaches around half a million children through more than 8,000 teachers in 20 countries.

Children learn by assembling visual coding blocks rather than writing code. "All the narratives are linked to the UN Sustainable Development Goals," explains pedagogical content creator André Ribeiro. "They create ethical content and learn to use technology for good."

Project manager Joana Miranda demonstrates a pupil's project in which robots work together to stop a forest fire. "Knowing how to use technology safely, responsibly and ethically is incredibly important," she says. Ubbu also aims to bridge the gender gap in technology. We're achieving a 50-50 audience in schools. Girls see role models and realise there are women in science, technology and engineering."

Making those skills accessible to every child is central to the company's mission. Through partnerships with companies and foundations, Ubbu is offered free to public schools in disadvantaged areas of Portugal.

At Amadora Oeste Agrupamento de Escolas’ primary school, on Lisbon's outskirts, teacher Isabel Cunha says the platform has transformed her classroom. "It captured my pupils' attention, and from there we explored many different topics," she says. "After only a year, they know how to use computers and tablets safely, how to navigate the web, I can already see great progress."

For nine-year-old Arwa, whom we follow home after school, coding is simply fun. For her father, the stakes are higher. "In 10 or 20 years, you won't be able to do anything without coding, programming or robotics," he says. "The people who know these things will be the future leaders."

title: London’s Bloomsbury Institute loses licence to sponsor international students
summary:
The Bloomsbury Institute has had its licence to sponsor international students revoked after failing to meet the Basic Compliance Assessment, the Home Office has confirmed in a statement.

The post London’s Bloomsbury Institute loses licence to sponsor international students appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The Home Office made clear that the assessment was carried out under thresholds that applied before the compliance standards were tightened on June 1 2026.

Under the new compliance framework handed down by the government, visa refusal rates must now be below 5%; course enrolment rate must be at least 95%, and course completion rate must be at least 85%. For assessments submitted from June 2027, the course completion threshold will rise to at least 90%.

“The Bloomsbury Institute would also have failed to meet the new, stricter standards. Failure to meet these standards represents a serious breach of its duties as an international student sponsor, and as a result, its licence was revoked on Wednesday August 5,” the Home Office statement read.

“Student sponsors must meet the standards required to retain their licence. Where standards are not met, the Home Office will take action to protect students and the integrity of the immigration system.”

The Home Office confirmed that the Bloomsbury Institute has been removed from the register of student sponsors and can no longer sponsor new international students under the student route.

Bloomsbury Institute said in a statement that it “acknowledges the Home Office’s decision to revoke its student sponsor licence following the Institute’s failure to meet two metrics of the annual Basic Compliance Assessment”.

“The assessment data related to a period prior to October 2025 following which significant changes in the leadership and management of the Institute and its processes have been implemented,” it continued.

“From October 2025, the Institute implemented a substantial program of improvements in governance and leadership. The Home Office recognised these steps in its decision, noting that the Institute had begun to respond to and address the identified failings from the earlier period,” the Institute’s statement read.

“In acknowledgement of those improvements, the Home Office reduced the length of time before the Institute may reapply for a Student Sponsor Licence from the standard two years to 18 months.”

The assessment data related to a period prior to October 2025 following which significant changes in the leadership and management of the Institute and its processes have been implemented

Bloomsbury Institute

The PIE News had previously reported on Bloomsbury Institute’s licence being suspended. At the time, a representative from the higher education provider said it was engaging “fully and constructively” with UKVI, reiterating the Institute’s commitment to satisfying “all regulatory obligations” in line with the new rules.

On August 6, announcing the revocation, the Home Office said its priority is to “minimise disruption for international students already enrolled at the Bloomsbury Institute”.

Similarly, the Institute said it is focusing on the welfare and continuity of study of currently enrolled sponsored students and said it is working closely with academic partners, the Office for Students and other relevant bodies “to ensure that all currently enrolled sponsored students are fully supported throughout this period”.

Existing students will not be affected immediately, and the Bloomsbury Institute will be permitted to continue teaching its current sponsored students “for a short period,” the Home Office statement read.

“A small number of students are expected to be unable to complete their course within that window and they will be supported to transfer to another institution. If they choose not to, they will need to apply for another visa route for which they are eligible or leave the UK,” it continued.

Alex Lock, head of immigration compliance at Anglia Ruskin University, commented on the development: “I am pleased that the Home Office have confirmed a teach out method for students and to allow students to transfer to other organisations, and I hope the best for the Institute’s staff and students at this time.

“It’s always really saddening when something like this happens and I hope that we, as a professional platform, can offer support, measured commentary, and take the lessons learned away,” he added.

Lock reminded his LinkedIn audience that the BCA has been “noted for a number of years as the correct process for license based discussions with the Home Office”.

“Whatever conversations meetings and discussion points that have occurred are for both the institute and the Home Office, and it is not appropriate for us to discuss or dig further in to this.”

Lock did acknowledge the Home Office statement as “sounding the alarm” for the wider higher education sector that the BCA metrics “will be fully enforced”.

title: US universities sell opportunity. A $100k OPT fee could change the product
summary:
News that the Trump administration is eyeing a $100,000 fee for OPT poses a serious risk to US international education, warns Richard T. Herman.

The post US universities sell opportunity. A $100k OPT fee could change the product appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Imagine you’re a talented engineering student admitted to graduate programs in both Boston and Toronto.

The tuition is comparable. The faculty are world-class. The research opportunities are outstanding. Both degrees could launch an international career.

But one country asks you to pay a reported $100,000 for the opportunity to begin that career after graduation.

The decision suddenly looks very different.

That is why recent Wall Street Journal reporting that the Trump administration is considering a $100,000 fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) deserves the attention of every university president, provost, enrolment manager, and government official involved in international education.

Whether or not the reported proposal ultimately becomes policy, it signals a fundamental reconsideration of one of America’s greatest higher education advantages.

As US Citizenship and Immigration Services explains, OPT allows eligible F-1 students to obtain temporary employment directly related to their field of study after graduation. For many international students, OPT is not simply an optional benefit added at the end of a degree. It is an integral part of the educational opportunity they are investing in.

That distinction matters.

American universities are not simply selling classroom instruction. They are selling an educational pathway: a globally respected degree combined with the opportunity to apply newly acquired knowledge in one of the world’s most dynamic and innovative economies. The ability to transition from study to professional experience has long distinguished American higher education from many of its competitors.

A six-figure OPT fee could fundamentally change that value proposition.

American universities are not simply selling classroom instruction. They are selling an educational pathway

International students evaluate universities differently than domestic applicants. They compare not only rankings and faculty, but also visa policies, post-study work opportunities, long-term career prospects, research opportunities, and total financial commitment. Every additional cost becomes part of an increasingly global calculation.

Students do not compare Harvard with Stanford alone. They compare the United States with Canada, the UK, Australia, Germany, Singapore, and every other country competing for the same exceptional talent.

According to the Institute of International Education’s Open Doors Report, the US hosted more than one million international students during the 2023/24 academic year, with India surpassing China as the largest country of origin. Those students strengthen campuses academically while enriching surrounding communities economically.

Their impact extends far beyond tuition.

According to NAFSA, international students contributed nearly $43 billion to the US economy and supported more than 355,000 American jobs during the 2024/25 academic year. They rent apartments, support local businesses, purchase goods and services, and sustain employment in communities across the country.

Perhaps even more important is what happens inside America’s research universities.

International graduate students are indispensable contributors in engineering, artificial intelligence, computer science, biotechnology, medicine, and other research-intensive disciplines. They help faculty secure grants, conduct laboratory research, publish scientific papers, and develop new technologies that strengthen American competitiveness.

When international enrolment declines, universities lose far more than tuition revenue. They lose research capacity. Employers lose access to highly-trained graduates already educated in American institutions. Regional innovation ecosystems lose future founders, inventors, and scientific collaborators.

Meanwhile, America’s competitors are pursuing the opposite strategy.

Canada’s Post-Graduation Work Permit Program is a central feature of its international education strategy. The United Kingdom’s Graduate visa was introduced to strengthen Britain’s attractiveness to global talent. Australia’s Temporary Graduate visa likewise promotes post-study employment as a competitive advantage.

These countries understand that international education is not merely an export industry. It is one of the world’s most effective long-term talent acquisition strategies.

The US understood that lesson for decades as well.

International students are not simply filling seats in classrooms. They are helping build America’s future workforce and innovation economy. Many go on to become physicians, scientists, engineers, professors, entrepreneurs, and business leaders whose contributions extend far beyond the years they spent on campus.

Research reinforces that point. Economists at the National Bureau of Economic Research have found that immigrants account for a disproportionately large share of US innovation and patent production, particularly in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. Research from the National Foundation for American Policy has likewise shown that immigrants have founded or co-founded a majority of America’s billion-dollar startup companies.

While those entrepreneurs arrived through different immigration pathways, many began their American journeys as international students, using American universities as the launching point for careers that generated new companies, new technologies, and new jobs.

Universities understand this dynamic. Today’s international graduate student may become tomorrow’s patent holder, principal investigator, startup founder, biotechnology executive, physician, professor, or Nobel laureate. The value they create often emerges years after graduation and continues for decades.

Reasonable people can debate immigration policy, visa integrity, and appropriate government fees. Every nation has the sovereign authority to determine who may study and work within its borders.

But policymakers should also recognize what universities have long understood.

OPT is not simply an immigration benefit. It has long been an important part of the competitive value proposition American higher education offers many international students, connecting world-class education with research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and economic opportunity.

A reported proposal to impose a $100,000 OPT fee should therefore be evaluated not only as an immigration measure, but also as a higher education policy, an innovation policy, and an economic competitiveness policy. At a time when other countries are expanding pathways designed to attract highly skilled graduates, the US should carefully consider whether substantially increasing the cost of launching a career here advances its long-term national interests.

The world’s brightest students will continue to pursue knowledge, develop new technologies, build companies, earn patents, and advance scientific discovery. The question is not whether tomorrow’s breakthroughs will happen, but where they will happen.

For generations, the US has distinguished itself by attracting talented students from around the world, educating them in world-class institutions, and giving many the opportunity to contribute to American research, industry, medicine, entrepreneurship, and public life. That openness has been one of America’s enduring competitive advantages.

Preserving that advantage is about more than immigration policy. It is about whether the United States intends to remain the world’s leading destination for talent, innovation, and discovery.

title: Gesichter statt Zielgruppen: Warum wir für die Wissenschaft Personas entwickeln
summary:
Vielen Weiterbildungsangeboten fehlt eine konkrete, klar eingegrenzte Zielgruppe. Personas können dabei helfen! Was man unter dem Begriff überhaupt versteht, und wie man das Prinzip für die digitale Wissenschaft anwenden kann, erklären Anja-Lisa Schroll und Christian Erlacher in diesem Blogbeitrag und im November auch in einem zweitägigen Workshop. 

The post Gesichter statt Zielgruppen: Warum wir für die Wissenschaft Personas entwickeln appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
„Zielgruppengerechte Weiterbildung“ – diesen Satz habe ich in den letzten Jahren in vermutlich jedem zweiten Schulungskonzept gelesen. Er klingt gut. Er verpflichtet zu nichts. Denn wer ist eigentlich „die Zielgruppe“? Die Doktorandin, die zum ersten Mal mit einer KI-gestützten Datenpipeline arbeitet? Der Bibliotheksreferent, der E-Learning-Formate betreut? Die Abteilungsleitung, die über Weiterbildungsbudgets entscheidet? Alle drei tauchen in Statistiken oft unter derselben Überschrift auf – und brauchen in Wahrheit völlig unterschiedliche Angebote.

Genau an diesem Punkt setzen wir in der Interessengruppe 4 „Personal, Aus- und Weiterbildung“ der Allianz der deutschen Wissenschaftsorganisationen an.

Am 19. & 20. November 2026 veranstalten wir gemeinsam mit dem Hochschulforum Digitalisierung in Bonn einen Workshop mit dem Titel „Zielgruppen verstehen – Personas & Kompetenzen für die digitale Wissenschaft.“ Ziel: aus abstrakten Zielgruppen konkrete, arbeitsfähige Personas machen – und daraus ableiten, welche digitalen Kompetenzen diese unterschiedlichen Personengruppen tatsächlich brauchen.

Der digitale Wandel verändert die Wissenschaftslandschaft spürbar schneller, als viele Personalentwicklungskonzepte mithalten können. Neue KI-Tools, veränderte Arbeit mit und an Daten, neue Formen der Zusammenarbeit – all das trifft auf Mitarbeitende mit sehr unterschiedlichen Rollen und sehr unterschiedlichem Vorwissen.

Wenn Weiterbildungsangebote trotzdem pauschal für „die Wissenschaftler:innen“ oder „das Verwaltungspersonal“ konzipiert werden, verpuffen sie. Zu allgemein für die einen, zu banal für die anderen.

Die Personamethode aus dem nutzerzentrierten Design bietet hier einen Ausweg. Statt mit Kategorien zu arbeiten, entwickeln wir fiktive, aber realitätsnahe Personen mit Namen, Aufgaben und typischen Alltagssituationen. Eine Persona wie „Digital Researcher“ oder „Scientific Manager“ lässt sich konkret befragen: Womit kämpft sie im Arbeitsalltag? Welche KI-Tools nutzt sie – und welche traut sie sich (noch) nicht zu? Das macht Kompetenzlücken sichtbar, die in generischen Bedarfsanalysen untergehen.

Tag 1 steht im Zeichen der Persona-Entwicklung. Die Gruppen erarbeiten und diskutieren Personas – wer sie ist, welche Aufgaben sie hat, wo ihre digitalen Kompetenzen liegen (sollten).

Tag 2 widmet sich der Kompetenzkartierung und der Weiterarbeit an den identifizierten Personas. Am Ende steht keine abstrakte Kompetenzliste, sondern eine Landkarte, die jede Institution direkt für ihre eigene Weiterbildungsplanung nutzen kann.
translated_text:
“Target group-oriented further training” – I have read this sentence in probably every other training concept in recent years. He sounds good. He doesn't commit to anything. Because who is actually “the target group”? The PhD student working with an AI-powered data pipeline for the first time? The library consultant who oversees e-learning formats? The department management that decides on training budgets? All three often appear in statistics under the same heading - and in reality they need completely different offers.

This is exactly where we come in in interest group 4 “Human resources, training and further education” of the Alliance of German Science Organizations.

On November 19th & 20th, 2026, together with the University Forum for Digitalization in Bonn, we will be organizing a workshop entitled “Understanding target groups – personas & competencies for digital science.” The goal: to turn abstract target groups into concrete, workable personas - and to derive from this which digital skills these different groups of people actually need.

Digital change is changing the scientific landscape noticeably faster than many personnel development concepts can keep up. New AI tools, changed work with and on data, new forms of collaboration – all of this affects employees with very different roles and very different prior knowledge.

If further training offers are nevertheless designed across the board for “scientists” or “administrative staff”, they will fall flat. Too general for some, too banal for others.

The persona method from user-centered design offers a way out here. Instead of working with categories, we develop fictional but realistic people with names, tasks and typical everyday situations. A persona such as “Digital Researcher” or “Scientific Manager” can be asked specifically: What do they struggle with in everyday work? Which AI tools does she use – and which ones does she not trust (yet)? This makes skills gaps visible that are lost in generic needs analyses.

Day 1 is dedicated to persona development. The groups develop and discuss personas – who they are, what their tasks are, where their digital skills (should) lie.

Day 2 is dedicated to competence mapping and further work on the identified personas. The end result is not an abstract list of skills, but rather a map that every institution can use directly for its own further training planning.

title: KI-Update Deep-Dive: Wie Schulen KI-Kompetenz systematisch vermitteln können
summary: Das AI Literacy Framework gibt Lehrkräften erstmals konkrete Lernszenarien zur KI-Vermittlung an die Hand – von der Grundschule bis zur Weiterbildung.
full_text:
Inhaltsverzeichnis

Vorbereitung auf PISA 2029

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Künstliche Intelligenz ist längst Teil des Alltags von Kindern und Jugendlichen. Doch wie gut verstehen sie, womit sie es dabei eigentlich zu tun haben? Und wie bereitet man eine Generation auf Technologien vor, die sich schneller verändern als Lehrpläne? Das AI Literacy Framwork will dafür die Richtung weisen. Es wurde von der Organisation für wirtschaftliche Zusammenarbeit und Entwicklung (OECD) gemeinsam mit der Europäischen Kommission und der US-amerikanischen Initiative Code.org entwickelt.

Ausschlaggebend war der Plan der OECD im Jahr 2029 erstmals Medien- und KI-Kompetenz im Rahmen der PISA-Erhebung abzufragen. "Wenn man 2029 KI-Kompetenz abfragen möchte, sollte man sich auch mit der Frage auseinandersetzen, was wir dafür tun können, dass die Ergebnisse möglichst gut sind", erklärt Florian Rampelt vom Stifterverband. Er ist Programmleiter für Future Skills & KI, Geschäftsstellenleiter der Lernplattform KI-Campus und war als Mitglied des internationalen Expertenteams an der Entwicklung beteiligt.

Die Expertengruppe arbeitete über eineinhalb Jahre an dem Rahmenwerk. Zwischendurch wurde ein erster Entwurf veröffentlicht, um Feedback aus der Bildungscommunity einzuholen. In Deutschland organisierte der Stifterverband mit Unterstützung der TÜV SÜD Stiftung eine eigene Arbeitsgruppe. Das Feedback aus offiziellen Konsultationen der EU-Mitgliedsländer sowie von KI-Initiativen, Bildungsakteuren und Lehrkräften floss dann in die Endversion ein. Anders als viele bestehende Konzepte verknüpft das so entstandene AI Literacy Framework Kompetenzanforderungen direkt mit konkreten Lernszenarien für den Unterricht.

Vier Kompetenzbereiche

Das Framework gliedert sich in vier Bereiche: Mit KI bewusst umgehen, KI kreativ anwenden, KI gezielt einsetzen und KI aktiv mitgestalten. Jede Kompetenz wird auf drei Progressionsstufen beschrieben – grundlegend, fortgeschritten und vertieft. "Die Szenarien sind ganz bewusst so gehalten, dass sie in unterschiedlichen Fächern genutzt und integriert werden können", betont Rampelt.

Der Grundlagenbereich behandelt die Frage, wo KI im Alltag bereits eine Rolle spielt. "Die erste Kompetenz ist die Rolle und den Einfluss von KI in verschiedenen Kontexten zu erkennen", erklärt Rampelt. Die Lernenden könnten zum Beispiel mit ihrer Lehrkraft „KI oder nicht“ spielen. „Anhand von Beispielen wie Smart Home-Geräten, sozialen Medien oder Apps können sie jedes Beispiel danach einordnen, ob es KI einsetzt oder nicht."

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Weitere Kompetenzen umfassen das Beschreiben von KI-Funktionsweisen sowie das Einordnen des Ressourcenverbrauchs von KI-Systemen. "Es ist wichtig, dass wir eben nicht alle ständig ChatGPT am Handy nutzen, um jede Frage zu beantworten", mahnt Rampelt. Mit jeder Nutzung generativer KI würden Ressourcen verbraucht, was vielen im Alltag nicht bewusst sei.

Podcast: KI-Update

Wie intelligent ist Künstliche Intelligenz eigentlich? Welche Folgen hat generative KI für unsere Arbeit, unsere Freizeit und die Gesellschaft? Im "KI-Update" von Heise bringen wir Euch gemeinsam mit The Decoder dreimal die Woche Updates zu den wichtigsten KI-Entwicklungen. Freitags beleuchten wir mit Experten die unterschiedlichen Aspekte der KI-Revolution.

Apple Podcasts

Google Podcasts

RSS-Feed

Spotify

KI-Update als Newsletter abonnieren

Zu unserem Partner: The Decoder

Materialien für Deutschland

Ethische Fragen ziehen sich durch das gesamte Framework. Auf der Wissensebene geht es etwa um Verzerrungen, sogenannte Biases, und deren gesellschaftliche Konsequenzen. Kritisches Denken wird auf der Kompetenzebene mit ethischen Aspekten verknüpft, während auf der Haltungsebene Verantwortungsbewusstsein als besonders notwendig erachtet wird. Zu einem verantwortungsvollen KI-Design gehörten laut Rampelt Prinzipien wie Fairness, Transparenz und Rechenschaftspflicht.

Für den deutschsprachigen Raum stellt der KI-Campus schon jetzt ergänzende Materialien bereit. "Wir glauben, dass für eine Nutzung auf Länder- und auf regionaler Ebene auch eine Kontextualisierung vor Ort notwendig ist", erklärt Rampelt. Über einen Ideenwettbewerb mit der TÜV SÜD Stiftung entwickeln Hochschulen und Schulen weitere eigene Umsetzungsideen. "Unser Ziel ist, schrittweise für die unterschiedlichen Kompetenzbereiche Online-Kurse und Bildungsmaterialien zur Verfügung zu stellen, die dann auch im Unterricht genutzt werden können", sagt Rampelt.

Empfohlener redaktioneller Inhalt

Mit Ihrer Zustimmung wird hier ein externer Podcast (Podigee GmbH) geladen.

Kurz nach der Veröffentlichung wurde das Framework in die KI-Verordnung der Europäischen Union aufgenommen. Es dient damit offiziell als Orientierungsrahmen für alle Organisationen und Unternehmen in Europa, die KI-Systeme nutzen.
translated_text:
Table of Contents

Preparing for PISA 2029

Read more after the ad

Artificial intelligence has long been part of the everyday lives of children and young people. But how well do they understand what they are actually dealing with? And how do you prepare a generation for technologies that are changing faster than curricula? The AI ​​Literacy Framework wants to point the way. It was developed by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) together with the European Commission and the US initiative Code.org.

The decisive factor was the OECD's plan to survey media and AI skills for the first time in 2029 as part of the PISA survey. “If you want to query AI competence in 2029, you should also consider the question of what we can do to ensure that the results are as good as possible,” explains Florian Rampelt from the Stifterverband. He is the program manager for Future Skills & AI, branch manager of the KI-Campus learning platform and was involved in the development as a member of the international team of experts.

The expert group worked on the framework for over a year and a half. In between, a first draft was published to obtain feedback from the educational community. In Germany, the donor association organized its own working group with the support of the TÜV SÜD Foundation. Feedback from official consultations with EU member states as well as from AI initiatives, education stakeholders and teachers was then incorporated into the final version. Unlike many existing concepts, the resulting AI Literacy Framework links competency requirements directly with concrete learning scenarios for teaching.

Four areas of competence

The framework is divided into four areas: dealing with AI consciously, applying AI creatively, using AI in a targeted manner and actively helping to shape AI. Each competency is described at three levels of progression – basic, advanced and in-depth. “The scenarios are deliberately designed so that they can be used and integrated in different subjects,” emphasizes Rampelt.
